recruiting_oncology.name: Vaccine Study for Dogs with Splenic Hemangiosarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo removal of the spleen, followed by standard care therapy in addition to the vaccine. The vaccine will be given over 6 visits approximately 3 weeks apart in addition to 6 chemotherapy visits. If appropriate, your dog will also receive boosters every 6 months. The chemotherapy visits will be scheduled 2 weeks prior to each vaccine visit. At each visit, blood will also be drawn to measure the immune response for study purposes.

recruiting_oncology.name: Pilot study of Frunevetmab (Solensia) and Meloxicam for palliative therapy of feline bone-invasive oral squamous cell carcinomas
recruiting_oncology.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinomas are a common oral cancer in cats. These tumors are locally aggressive and associated with tissue and 
bone destruction. The average survival time of cats with this oral tumor type is reported to be 3 months or less, even after
aggressive treatment. Many owners elect to pursue palliative (pain relief) care options rather than cancer treatments. However, 
there can be challenges with palliative care as the selection of pain medication for cats is limited and most require oral
administration. There is an unmet need for pain medications that are safe and effective at maintaining a good quality of life for
cats with oral tumors. Therefore, the goal of this study is to evaluate a currently available injectable drug, which is marketed for the treatment of arthritis pain in cats, for its ability to also provide relief of pain associated with oral cancers.

recruiting_oncology.name: Pilot study evaluating palbociclib in dogs with melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, mammary carcinoma, or anal sac adenocarcinoma
recruiting_oncology.description: This is a clinical trial evaluating the use of a new chemotherapy drug, palbociclib, in tumor-bearing drugs with certain cancers. Palbociclib is currently used in humans with breast cancer and other tumors. It has been given to laboratory dogs to report some pharmacokinetic and toxicity data in preclinical trials. The intent of the clinical trial is to measure drug levels in dogs with cancer to determine a recommended prescription dose. We will also describe side effects and, while not a primary endpoint of the study, tumor response.

recruiting_oncology.name: Comparative Molecular Analysis for Acquired Toceranib Resistance in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors
recruiting_oncology.description: The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting dogs diagnosed with non-resectable cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs) for a clinical research study. The purpose of this trial is to investigate novel biological characteristics associated with toceranib phosphate (Palladia®) resistance in canine cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (cMCTs).

recruiting_oncology.name: Trametinib for Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description: The purpose of this research is to investigate a new anti-cancer drug, trametinib, that specifically ‘targets’ growth signals found in cancer cells from companion (pet) dogs. This study will determine the anti-tumor efficacy of trametinib in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma. We will measure and document how much the cancer shrinks upon treatment, and how the drug helps improve the patients’ outcome and life expectancy. Additionally, the study will test whether markers in the genes within the tumor can predict the response from treatment, which in the future can help select those dogs that are more likely to respond positively to treatment. Finally, in a simple blood test we will determine whether effective drug levels are present in the patient.

recruiting_oncology.name: Incidence of hypercoagulability and thromboembolism in dogs with surgically treated primary hepatocellular and adrenal neoplasia
recruiting_oncology.description:
The goal of this study is to characterize the hemostatic abnormalities in dogs with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer undergoing surgical removal and to determine when their hypercoagulability (increased tendency for blood to clot) resolves post-operatively. Additionally, we aim to determine the incidence of thromboembolism (blood clots) in hypercoagulable patients diagnosed with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer following tumor removal.


Dogs with suspected primary hepatocellular or adrenal neoplasia will undergo standard-of-care procedures, including blood work (CBC, chemistry, and PT/PTT) and CT of the abdomen. Upon enrollment, a TEG and fibrinogen level will be obtained before surgery for the study. Dogs will return in 10-14 days for re-check full-body CT and blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, PLT, fibrinogen). Dogs will return in 15-21 days for re-check blood work. Dogs will continue to return for recheck blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, fibrinogen, and PLT) until their hypercoagulability, based on an elevated TEG G-value, resolves.


If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 10-14 day post-surgery visit, they will be asked to come back for 3 and/or 4-week post-surgery visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 4-week post-surgery visit, it will present as needed for 6, 8,12, and/or 16-week post-operative visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 16-week post-operative visit, blood work re-checks will move to a monthly schedule until resolution is achieved. No future visits are required once a dog becomes normocoagulable. No future visits are required, and monthly blood work will discontinue if a dog remains hypercoagulable at 6 months post-operative (day 182).


The study will cover the cost of your dog's pre-operative chest and post-operative abdominal and chest computed tomography (CT) scan. Additionally, the study will cover the cost of each recheck examination fee and the cost of performing blood work (TEG, PCV/TS, platelet count, and fibrinogen) pre-and post-operatively.


Routine blood work (PT/PTT, CBC, chemistry panel, blood type prior to surgery) will not be covered by the study. The study does not cover the cost of your dog's other preoperative workup (primary tumor biopsy/FNA, pre-operative abdominal CT, thoracic radiographs, etc.), primary tumor removal, hospitalization, post-operative care, or additional oncologic care (radiation therapy or chemotherapy). Costs associated with adverse events (including but not limited to hematoma, and incisional complications) are not covered by the study.

recruiting_oncology.name: CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs
recruiting_oncology.description: Osteosarcoma (OS) is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that have macroscopic metastases to the lungs. CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells are a modified version of a T cell, a type of immune cell, that alters them so they can target and destroy cancer cells. Dogs have been previously treated with CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells at other institutions and the treatment has been well-tolerated, but the new CAR T cells being evaluated in this trial have not been evaluated in dogs with cancer, though safety studies were done in healthy dogs, without side effects. The goal of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of canine CAR T cells, which will be generated by gene modification of your dogs white blood cells, and then infused back into your dog by an intravenous catheter. In order to help the CAR T cells expand in the body more effectively, your dog will also have to be treated with bone marrow suppressing drugs (fludarabine and cyclophosphamide) for 2 days before the CAR T cells are given back. To help increase the effectiveness of the CAR T cells once they are recruited to the tumor tissues, dogs will be treated daily with oral losartan and propranolol before and after CAR T administration.

recruiting_oncology.name: Clinical Testing of Canine T cells Engineered to Target Osteosarcoma and Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Combination with Oral Immunotherapy
recruiting_oncology.description:
The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the safety and anti-cancer activity of fibroblast activation protein (FAP) targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, alone or in combination with orally administered immunotherapy drugs, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. FAP is a protein that is expressed on the surface of tumor cell and can be recognized by a T cell. CAR T cells are when a patient’s own cancer fighting white blood cells are modified to express a receptor which binds a specific molecule expressed on the surface of a tumor cell. The two oral immunotherapy drugs being used in combination with FAP CAR T cells (losartan and toceranib [Palladia]) have already been extensively evaluated in a prior trial in dogs with bone cancer and have demonstrated considerable anti-cancer activity, with minimal toxicity. Studies in rodent models of cancer and in vitro in human and canine OS cell lines have indicated that FAP CAR T cells can exert robust killing of canine OS cells and may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. Therefore, this trial is designed to determine whether FAP CAR T cells are safe alone and in combination with losartan and toceranib, and if losartan and toceranib can improve tumor infiltration of FAP CAR T cells.


At the start of the study, dogs will have blood drawn (~3 ½ tablespoons) to be used for generation of the CAR T cells. Dogs will also be sedated to have a small sample of their tumor taken for study purposes. They will return 10 days later for an exam, bloodwork, and for oral chemotherapy to reduce the number of normal lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) to maximize the effectiveness of the CAR T cells. A second dose of chemotherapy will be given at home by the owner the following day. Dogs will then return 14 days after the initial visit for an exam, blood and urine tests, blood collection for study purposes, and CAR T cell infusion. The infusion is given over 15 minutes, and then dogs will stay in the hospital until the end of the day for monitoring. Dogs will return 3 and 7 days later for an exam, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Fourteen days after the CAR T infusion, the tumor will be removed surgically. Visits will be required 2 and 6 weeks after surgery for an exam, blood/urine tests, and blood collection for the study. The study is complete after the visit 6 weeks post-surgery (total study duration of 10 weeks).


Some dogs enrolled in the study will receive two oral immune modulating drugs (toceranib and losartan) for the first ~4 weeks of the study. These will be given at home by the owners 1-2 times daily. Owners will know ahead of time whether or not dogs will be receiving these drugs.

recruiting_oncology.name: Canine Liver Tumor Study
recruiting_oncology.description:
North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine is currently enrolling canine patients that have 1-2 liver tumors into a clinical trial that is using a new therapy called INSPIRE, which uses electrical pulses to safely destroy the cells within a tumor.


This study has two treatment group:


One group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and their tumors are eligible for surgical resection, the patients in this group will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment followed by liver lobectomy a week later to remove the tumors.


The second group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary Hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and the tumors are not eligible for surgical resection, patients will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment. Patients will then be monitored over a 9-month period which includes five recheck appointments, during which patients will receive a CT scan and bloodwork to monitor the tumors.

recruiting_oncology.name: Treating Metastatic Cancer with PD-1 inhibitor and Targeted Immunotherapy
recruiting_oncology.description:
Metastatic disease prevents a unique clinical setting especially when the patients is still stable. Options are limited for treatment but may include oral and IV chemotherapy options. With the advent of PD-1 inhibitors, we are now looking to combine the inhibitor with either Telomerase or HER2 immunotherapy in combination as the combined therapies should improve response while minimizing adverse effects and battling the cancer through specific mechanisms.


Trends Cancer 2023 Jul;9(7):543-553.

 doi: 10.1016/j.trecan.2023.04.002. Epub 2023 Apr 27.

Immune mechanisms of toxicity from checkpoint inhibitors

S Jennifer Wang 1, Stephanie K Dougan 2, Michael Dougan 3


Abstract

Immunotherapy has changed the treatment landscape for cancer over the past decade. Inhibitors of the immune checkpoint proteins cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen (CTLA)-4, programmed death (PD)-1, and PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) can induce durable remissions in a subset of patients with metastatic disease. However, these treatments can be limited by inflammatory toxicities that can affect any organ system in the body and in some cases can be life threatening. Considerable progress has been made in understanding the drivers of these toxicities as well as effective management strategies. Further research into understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms that drive toxicity will enable better prediction of toxicity and development of optimized therapies for these toxicities that avoid interfering with antitumor immunity. In this review, we discuss our current understanding of the inflammatory toxicities from immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and propose optimal treatment strategies for these toxicities.


Clinical protocol: Patients will be treated with standard of care anti-PD1 SOP: Administered as an intravenous (IV) infusion over at least 30 minutes either manually or with a constant rate syringe pump. Repeat administration every 2 weeks for up to 10 treatments. Antihistamine administered intramuscularly (IM) 15-30 minutes before treatment to prevent or reduce the severity of infusion-related reactions, 20-30 minutes following administration, patients will be sedated with propofol, dexdomitor and O2 via intubation for GET (see below).


GET: DNA Plasmid: The N-10-4B electrode to be inserted into the cranialis tibialis after immediate injection of dTERT or dHER2 DNA/plasmid. Minimal bleeding to be controlled with direct pressure.


Antisedan to be administered IM.


*Regarding the use of this technology (gene-electrotransfer or GET) as the method for vaccine delivery, numerous studies, including the one below, support the improved immune response compared to injections under the skin or in muscle.


Pharmaceutics. 2023 Jul; 15(7): 1981.

Published online 2023 Jul 19. doi: 10.3390/pharmaceutics15071981

PMCID: PMC10385748

recruiting_oncology.name: Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
Oral melanoma is a highly aggressive disease with poor outcomes and no effective treatments. Our recent research has shown that a weakened form of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is safe, and can trigger strong anti-tumor effects.


By injecting a small amount of this weakened virus directly into the tumor, we aim to activate the dog's immune system to fight the cancer. Additionally, we will collect and expand immune cells from the tumor, as these cells are more likely to recognize and attack cancer cells. These enhanced immune cells will then be reinfused into the patient to target existing or potential metastatic disease.


To evaluate our therapy, we will first perform a tumor biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and analyze the immune cells already present (Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes). We will then inject the tumor with the weakened virus. One week later, the tumor will be surgically removed, and immune cells from the cancer will be expanded for future use if metastases are present or develop later. After treatment, we will closely monitor the patients through periodic blood tests and imaging (CT scans) every three months.


A small group of dogs (randomly selected) will be the control, and while not receiving the virus injection, they will have their immune cells extracted from the tumor and expanded to be reinfused in case of progressive disease.


Cost of tumor biopsy, two CT imaging sessions, trial-related blood work, the viral reagent and injections, the collection priming and reinjection of the immune cells. Additionally, participating dogs are eligible to receive a $800 post-trial incentive.

recruiting_oncology.name: SOLID study for lymphoma in dogs
recruiting_oncology.description: The Ethos Stratification of Outcomes for Lymphoma In Dogs (Ethos-SOLID) study is a clinical trial focused on better understanding the genetics behind canine lymphoma. By studying changes in the DNA of these cancers, researchers hope to identify patterns that could lead to more personalized treatment options. The goal is to find markers in the tumor and blood that can help predict how the cancer will behave and guide more effective treatment decisions.

recruiting_oncology.name: COSMyc- IT Trial- Canine Oncology Study for Myc Inhibition Tolerability Trial
recruiting_oncology.description:
Myc (a family of transcription factors encompassing c-, N-, and L-Myc) is a pleiotropic, evolutionarily conserved transcription factor. Myc is one of the most frequently amplified oncogenes in most (perhaps all) human cancers (Dang 2012, Whitfield 2017) and often correlates with aggressiveness of the disease (Wolfer 2010; Lee 2015). In breast cancer, Myc is overexpressed in 30–50% of high-grade tumors, is markedly elevated in triple-negative breast cancer and even further elevated in tumors that display a drug-resistant phenotype (Fallah 2017). In non-small cell lung cancer, Myc amplification is found in up to 30% of malignancies (Ahmadzada 2018; Kalkat 2017).


A new novel peptide that inactivates Myc has been developed and is currently in human trials. The goal of this study is to determine the tolerability and feasibility of administering this novel peptide to dogs with cancer to inform future efficacy studies.

recruiting_oncology.name: Radiotherapy Trial for Metastatic Bone Cancer in Dogs
recruiting_oncology.description:
Purpose of the study: 

This study seeks to determine whether a new treatment can be safe and effective to stop osteosarcoma or bone cancer that has spread or metastasized beyond the tumor in the limb.  Your pet will receive a small amount of a radiotherapy, which consists of a radioactive compound linked to a monoclonal antibody, called “225-Actinium 3F8 (225Ac-3F8) in a vein. We will then do a specialized type of imaging called Single Photo Emission Computed Tomography(SPECT) combined with a computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan to determine whether your pet’s tumor takes up this agent. We will also take samples of blood, urine, and feces to try and determine the maximum dose that your dog can tolerate. We may then give an additional dose of 225Ac-3F8 in a vein several days later to treat your dog. We will follow-up with sampling of the blood and another specialized imaging called Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET-CT) at approximately 40 days after treatment to determine your dog's response.

recruiting_oncology.name: Enrolling Dogs with Invasive Bladder Cancer
recruiting_oncology.description: NC State Medical Oncology is enrolling patients for a clinical trial of an experimental immunotherapy for the treatment of bladder cancer. The primary purpose of this study is to investigate the safety and immune-stimulating properties of a novel therapy being developed at NCSU.

recruiting_oncology.name: Combination chemotherapy (Doxorubicin-Temozolomide with or without propranolol) in dogs with Hemangiosarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin and temozolomide with or without propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. A sister drug to Temozolomide, DTIC, has shown promise in improving survival times, however side effects and the long administration times have created challenges with the use of DTIC in dogs. Temozolomide is administered orally and is historically well tolerated in dogs. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments and improved tolerability. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

recruiting_oncology.name: Combinatorial Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer
recruiting_oncology.description:
Background and purpose


For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. This agent is an immunotherapeutic drug (anti-PDL1) bound to a fluorophore. This drug would be given 2X before treatment (surgery or other).


Through this study we will determine if this drug can allow us to see residual cancer cells during surgery (differentiate cancer from healthy tissue) and if treatment of the tumor before surgery with the drug can improve the local anti-tumor immune response (decrease in percent viable cells in the tumor).


If successful this could overall vastly improve our ability to treat oral cancer in dogs.


What happens in this study


  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical examination, full blood work, urinalysis
  2. A pre-operative biopsy performed at enrollment, to confirm squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma
  3. Intravenous administration of the anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 theranostic probe twice before surgery
  4. Near infrared fluorescence Imaging performed at 8 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours after probe delivery
  5. Repeat biopsy or curative intent surgery after the second anti-PDL1-IRDye 800 probe administration
  6. Follow-up visits at 7 days and 4 weeks

Study number: VCCT-26-008

recruiting_oncology.name: Pilot Study for a New Quasiorganelle Therapy in Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside. Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.


The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment. Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.

The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.

Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.


Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

Please note: All treatments and relevant follow up must be performed at Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine. Investigational treatment will not be sent to outside clinics.

recruiting_oncology.name: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)
recruiting_oncology.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.

recruiting_oncology.name: Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) Cancer Treatment
recruiting_oncology.description:
Targeted Electrochemotherapy (ECT) treatment consists of delivering a low dose of chemotherapy, followed by short electric pulses to the cancer. With the delivery of the electric pulses, cell membranes are transiently opened allowing chemotherapy directly into the cell. Treatment may be repeated over the course of weeks or months to achieve regression of large lesions. Targeted Electrochemotherapy employs lower dosages of chemotherapeutic drugs than standard chemotherapy protocols. In the clinical use of electrochemotherapy, side effects are uncommon and patients maintain or improve quality of life. Currently, Electrochemotherapy in animals is under a short anesthesia and with a variety of electrodes available to us, many tumor types and locations (including internal cancers) are candidates for this therapy.


Targeted Electrochemotherapy, in veterinary oncology (dogs, cats, exotics and horses), has been dominated by centers in Europe and South America. Here at Veterinary Oncology Services, there is not a location where cancer may not be treated. It may be used for a wide variety of tumors including:


Sarcomas in the mouth, eyelid, foot pad, skin or distal limb and their scars, Feline vaccine-associated fibrosarcoma before and after surgery, Melanoma in the mouth, eyelid or foot pad, Squamous cell carcinoma in mouth, eyelid, ear, nasal planum or foot pad, Incompletely resected soft tissue sarcomas where aggressive surgical treatment would necessitate amputation, Localized cutaneous lymphoma in dogs or cats, Local control of mast cell tumors including scars, Perianal & rectal tumors, prostate, pancreas, Hepatocellular carcinomas/adenomas, Perianal tumors, Sarcoids, sarcoma and squamous cell carcinomas in horses, Superficial tumors on exotics (small mammals, birds & zoo animals) If you have a patient that may benefit from this therapy, please do not hesitate to contact us at 845 205 2768 or info@petcancerinformation.com. recruiting_oncology.name: Combination of electrochemotherapy and gene therapy with canine IL-12
recruiting_oncology.description:
Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is an advanced treatment in veterinary oncology. It has been routinely used in dogs for treating mast cell tumors, carcinomas and soft tissue sarcomas, in cats for SCC, carcinomas and sarcomas and in horses for sarcoid tumors. ECT is a local ablative technique which has a good local anti-tumor control in dogs (up to 70%) and in cats (up to 80%) and in horses up to 100% but limited impact on distant tumors and metastasis. Therefore, there is a need for a combination therapy which could provide local control with a systemic effect to battle cancer spread. Interleukin 12 is a potent immune stimulator that works by increasing IFN gamma which has an anti-tumor effects through the activation of cytotoxic cells such as natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. IL-12 also up-regulates antigen presenting cells making the tumor cells recognizable to the immune system. Several clinical studies have already been performed treating different canine tumors by electro-genetransfer with a plasmid encoding IL-12. Results showed increased systemic IL-12 and IFN gamma with an effect on distant metastasis .

Procedure: The treatment consists of electrochemotherapy with bleomycin (intravenously) and gene-electrotransfer (GET) of IL-12 (intra-lesional). The treatment will be performed in patients under a short general anesthesia. Depending on the tumor volume and the response the treatments will be repeated every 3-4 weeks. Responses will be followed with physical exam and imaging (X-rays or CT). Electrochemotherapy will be performed using direct intra-tumoral application of IL-12 (2mg per patient) and the intravenous application of bleomycin (standard dose). The study is based on multiple publications showing benefit with this combination with control of the cancer including metastasis and minimal to no adverse effects to the patients.

recruiting_oncology.name: Exploring a Nonoparticle-enabled Treatment of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Cats
recruiting_oncology.description:
For veterinary patients, surgery is the primary treatment for many tumour types. Surgery may not always be the best option for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) as it is challenging to obtain adequate clear surgical margins and often, the disease reoccurs. Adjuvant therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy and palliative options are ineffective or poorly tolerated and do not improve the overall survival rate of cats with OCSCC. We need to make improvements to staging and treatment.

PORPHYSOMES (pPs) are a novel nanomedicine developed and supplied by Professor Dr Gang Zheng’s Laboratory (University Health Network, Toronto). These particles are delivered intravenously (in a local vein through a catheter) and concentrate in areas with tumour cells (either the primary tumour location or where the cancer has spread (metastatic site). pPs can be used to highlight the tumour by using a specialized technique called near-infrared fluorescence imaging (NIRF). This equipment allows for image-guided surgery, tumour margin assessment and lymph node staging. pPs can also be used to in combination with photoablation – photodynamic therapy (PDT) to deliver treatment directly to the tumour. 

 

pPs-enabled therapies can have an immediate impact on cancer management providing better patient outcomes. This study offers a novel approach to the treatment of OCSCC in cats. The use of pPs is ground-breaking translational research and the information gained will be used to treat future dogs, cats and humans with cancer. A human clinical trial is planned to be conducted in 2024.

recruiting_oncology.name: Vaccine study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma
recruiting_oncology.description: The enrolled dogs will undergo amputation or radiation of the affected limb followed immediately by vaccination every 3 weeks. The vaccine will be given over 6 visits approximately 3 weeks apart in addition to 6 chemotherapy visits. If appropriate your dog will also receive boosters every 6 months after completing the initial series. The chemotherapy visits will be scheduled 2 weeks prior to each vaccine visit. At each visit, blood will also be drawn to measure the immune response for study purposes.

recruiting_oncology.name: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
recruiting_oncology.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.


Once enrolled, dogs will have blood and urine collected for bone breakdown markers followed by 3 doses (or fractions) of SBRT. On the third and final fraction, dogs will receive the first dose of standard of care chemotherapy (carboplatin). Two weeks after chemotherapy, your dog will need to have a complete blood count performed to assess response to chemotherapy as well as blood and urine collected for the bone breakdown markers. At each dose of chemotherapy, a total of 6, blood and urine will be collected to assess trends in these markers. At the time of the final chemotherapy treatment, an additional dual energy CT will be performed to assess the changes that happen to the bone after treatment. Once chemotherapy is complete, it is recommended that your dog return every 8 weeks for chest x-rays; blood and urine will be collected for the study at the 1st 3 visits post-chemotherapy. At any change in lameness or concern for progression of disease, it is expected that your dog will return to CSU for assessment and evaluation of the bone markers.

recruiting_oncology.name: Dose escalation study for a novel STING agonist in tumor-bearing dogs
recruiting_oncology.description:
Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade. This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.

The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-cancer properties of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade.


There will be two study groups:


The first group of patients (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will visit their primary veterinarians one week later for blood sampling. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.


The second group of dogs (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 with PD-1 blockade. Their tumor will measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return one week later for tumor measurements, blood sampling, and anti-PD-1 infusion. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second CMP-002 infusion. Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.

recruiting_oncology.name: Mammary tumors in cats
recruiting_oncology.description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind following removal of mammary tumors in client-owned cats undergoing surgery. This technology has been used successfully in human breast cancer surgery, providing microscopic assessment of surgical margins within minutes. Identifying a rapid and thorough imaging method to detect any remaining cancer cells during surgery for mammary tumors will support targeted treatment management decisions and improve outcomes for cats and dogs with cancer.


Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive a $70 credit to their account to cover the costs of the histopathology evaluation.

recruiting_oncology.name: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
recruiting_oncology.description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.

recruiting_oncology.name: Immune treatment of Canine Bone Cancer
recruiting_oncology.description: Dogs with bone cancer or osteosarcoma of the limbs will be first assessed with a specialized imaging called 18F-FDG PET-CT to determine that the tumor is limited to the leg. Once enrolled, the dog will be treated with an immunotherapy directly in the tumor followed by chemotherapy the next 1-2 days prior to amputation. The goal of this therapy is to increase the immune response to the tumor. After amputation, treatment with standard chemotherapy will be augmented with an immune checkpoint inhibitor. At three, six, and twelve months after amputation, non-invasive imaging will be performed to look for spread of osteosarcoma. All treatments performed at the Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, MD are free-of-charge. The immune checkpoint inhibitor will be provided free-of-charge. The owner will need to make arrangements for amputation and chemotherapy with a surgeon and medical oncologist, respectively.

recruiting_oncology.name: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
recruiting_oncology.description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.

recruiting_oncology.name: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
recruiting_oncology.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.


Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses after radiation treatment. At that time, patients with persistent tumors are eligible to receive $1000 towards the cost of standard chemotherapy treatment.

recruiting_oncology.name: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.

recruiting_oncology.name: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
recruiting_oncology.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.


IACUC: 24619

Study number: VCCT-26-014


The study will provide $3000 toward initial diagnotic tests or radiation therapy for your pet.

recruiting_oncology.name: Radiation Treatment for Cats with Small Cell GI Lymphoma
recruiting_oncology.description:
Feline small cell gastrointestinal lymphoma (SCGL) is a common cancer in cats causing chronic weight loss, vomiting, and diarrhea. While standard effective treatments involve daily pills, not all cats will tolerate these medications. This study investigates a pill-free alternative with three daily radiation treatments (RT). To attempt to ensure the treatments are safe for the cats’ gastrointestinal tracts, a specialized delivery method that administers the radiation more slowly will be utilized. Cats with a diagnosis of SCGL who have experienced symptoms for more than six weeks and who have not yet received treatment can be enrolled. After radiation treatment, we will check how well the cats respond to treatment and watch for side effects. Additionally, we will test stool samples from the cats during the study to help us learn about the healthy and harmful bacteria in the cats’ intestines. The goal of this study is to find a treatment that is easy to complete, safe, helpful, and improves the quality of life for cats with SCGL.


At the beginning of the study, cats will receive three daily doses of radiation for a total of 6 Gy delivered to the entire gastrointestinal tract. Owners will provide stool samples prior to radiation and at recheck appointments performed 1-week, 1-month, 3-months, and 6-months following RT. At recheck appointments, cats will undergo a physical examination to assess clinical progress following treatment. At home, owners weigh their cats on a provided scale and complete an online survey regarding their clinical progress once weekly for a month, then once monthly for 6 months following radiation therapy.

recruiting_oncology.name: Enhanced Ethanol Ablation for Feline Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
recruiting_oncology.description: Some cancer patients have a poor prognosis, despite intensive multimodal therapy (e.g., surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy). In other cases, these treatments are likely to improve outcome but are inaccessible (e.g., financial, scheduling and/or geographical limitations). Thus, there is an immense need for treatments that offer effective tumor control and palliation, and that ideally can be given at low-cost in the primary care setting. We have recently demonstrated proof-of-concept for a low-cost effective option, called enhanced ethanol ablation. Ethanol ablation (intratumoral injectionof pure ethanol) was originally used for human liver cancer, achieving survival rates similar to surgical resection for small tumors. However, conventional ethanol ablation is ineffective for superficial, large, and/or poorly encapsulated lesions, and requires large injection volumes. Enhanced ethanol ablation involves controlled injection of an ethyl cellulose- ethanol mixture directly into the tumor. When mixed with ethyl cellulose, a water-insoluble ethanol-based gel is formed. We have shown this caused complete regression in 7 of 7 chemically-induced tumors in the hamster oral cavity while dramatically reducing the required injection volume. Now, we will perform a pilot study to evaluate safety and efficacy in feline oral squamous cell carcinomas, which serves as a model for other large, superficial and invasive tumors. Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma (mandibular and maxillary) will be enrolled. They will have basic staging tests performed, and then undergo anesthesia for a intratumoral injection of ethyl cellulose-ethanol. The tumor will be imaged using CT, before and after injection. Cats will be hospitalized overnight for observation, after this first injection. They will then return for periodic recheck exams to evaluate for toxicity and changes in tumor size. Depending on response to the first injection, cats may be eligible for up to 2 booster injections. Cats will be dismissed from the study at the time of local disease progression, or after 6 months of follow-up.

recruiting_oncology.name: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)
recruiting_oncology.description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Ethos-PUSH embarks on a journey to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubator of scientific innovation, Ethos Discovery has developed the most innovative scientific portfolio in the field of animal health and delivers answers to our clinical research questions through rigorous clinical trials made available to pet patients. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. We are agnostic to the source of good ideas and uniquely positioned, with the support of Ethos Veterinary Health, to reach patients and doctors nationally and partner with key leaders in their field internationally. This flexibility provides us the opportunity to pursue impactful research that will make a difference where it is most important, at the point of care and for the benefit of patients and families in the community.

recruiting_oncology.name: Minimally Invasive Metastasectomy in Canines (MIMIC) Trial
recruiting_oncology.description: Following surgical removal of the primary tumor and treatment with chemotherapy, the spread of cancer to the lungs (metastasis) is the most common cause of mortality in dogs with many tumors. A distinctive feature of lung metastases in human patients is the surprising benefit that can result from surgical removal of the lung metastases. The use of surgery to manage lung metastases in dogs has been described but is not commonly used due to the presumed post-surgical complications associated with conventional open chest surgery (thoracotomy). Innovations in minimally invasive surgery have created a new opportunity to include surgical removal of lung metastases with a reduced potential of complications when compared to the conventional thoracotomy techniques. Conventional thoracotomy techniques can be replaced by thoracoscopy, a surgical technique using miniature incisions in the chest to allow for removal of lung metastases with the assistance of a magnified video camera. This approach has the potential to significantly minimize the pain, potential complications, and recovery time in patients compared to what is observed with conventional thoracotomy techniques. Using minimally invasive surgery, specifically video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), we predict patients will be recovered from the procedure within 2 days and will be able to begin to return to normal life. The goal of our study is to assess the feasibility and tolerability of VATS for lung metastasis and eventually deliver this care as an outpatient procedure.
